title: David Among the Philistines
summary: Convinced that Saul will eventually kill him, David takes his six hundred men and their families to Achish, the Philistine king of Gath. Achish gives him the town of Ziklag, and for sixteen months David raids desert peoples to the south, killing everyone so that no one can report him, while telling Achish he has been raiding Judah. Achish comes to trust him completely.
story: The chapter follows directly from Saul's blessing in chapter 26, and it is striking how little that blessing reassures David. He speaks only to himself, not to God, and decides that his only safety lies in leaving Israel altogether. Earlier he had fled to this same Achish and escaped only by pretending to be mad (21:10-15); now he comes as a mercenary captain with a private army. The move works: Saul stops hunting him. But it also traps David in a double life. He must look like a loyal vassal of the Philistines while secretly protecting Judah, and the deception will soon put him in an impossible position when the Philistines march against Israel (chapters 28 and 29). The chapter is a dark interlude in the rise of the future king.
historical:
Gath was one of the five Philistine city-states and is generally identified with Tell es-Safi, a large site on the edge of the coastal plain where excavations led by Aren Maeir have shown it was a major city in this period. Achish son of Maoch is its king; Philistine rulers were usually called lords, but the narrator uses the Hebrew word for king for Achish. Ziklag lay somewhere in the western Negev, the dry southern region; its exact location is debated among several proposed sites.

The notice that Ziklag belongs to the kings of Judah to this day (verse 6) implies that the writer lived when there were distinct kings of Judah, after the kingdom divided around 930 BC. The peoples David raids, the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites, were seminomadic groups of the desert south toward Shur, on the border of Egypt. The southern Geshurites are distinct from the Aramean kingdom of Geshur in the north. The Jerahmeelites and Kenites, whose regions David pretends to have raided, were clans closely allied with Judah, which is why Achish believes the raids have made David hated by his own people.
cultural:
Mercenary service was common in the ancient Near East. Kings valued experienced soldiers without local loyalties, and a band like David's, fighting men with their families and flocks, could be settled on the frontier in return for military service and a share of plunder. Giving David a town of his own away from the royal city suited both men: Achish gained a buffer on his southern border, and David gained freedom from close watching.

Raiding for livestock and goods was a normal part of life in the desert fringe, and the Amalekites in particular were remembered in Israel as old enemies who had attacked Israel after the exodus (Exodus 17, Deuteronomy 25:17-19). David's practice of leaving no one alive, however, is explained entirely by his need for secrecy, so that no survivor could tell Achish where he had really been. The plunder he takes (flocks, herds, donkeys, camels, and clothing) is the wealth of pastoral peoples, the same kind of spoil David will later share with the towns of Judah (30:26-31).
literary: The chapter is short and cool in tone. The narrator reports and does not evaluate. The opening verse gives us David's inner speech, and it is notable for what is missing: unlike chapter 23, where David repeatedly inquired of the LORD, there is no prayer, no priest, no ephod, and no word from God. The rest of the chapter is built on the gap between what David does and what he says. Achish's repeated question, “What have you raided today?”, receives false answers, and the chapter ends with Achish's own inner speech, which is completely wrong: he thinks David has become an utter stench to Israel and will be his servant forever. The reader knows better, and the irony sets up the crisis of the next chapters.

outline.t: David despairs of safety and goes to Achish
David's raids and his deception of Achish

doctrines.note: David's words in verse 1 show fear winning out over the promises he has received from Samuel, Jonathan, Abigail, and even Saul. The chapter is an honest picture of faith under long strain, and of how a believer can make a decision out of exhaustion without ever asking God.

Even in David's compromised choices God keeps his purpose moving. Ziklag becomes a base from which David builds ties with the towns of Judah (30:26-31), and his exile keeps him away from the battle in which Saul dies, so that no one can accuse him of Saul's death.

words.note: Baash, to stink, and in its causative form to make oneself odious. Achish believes David has made himself an utter stench to his people. The same idiom is used when Jacob's sons make him odious to the Canaanites (Genesis 34:30) and when the Ammonites realize they have become odious to David (2 Samuel 10:6). Achish is sure David's bridges to Israel are burned; the reader knows they are not.

Pashat, to strip, and by extension to make a raid. The word pictures raiders stripping a territory of its goods. It describes David's attacks here, and later the Amalekite raid on Ziklag (30:1, 14), which will turn the same kind of violence back onto David's own town.

Mishpat, usually justice or judgment, here meaning custom or regular practice. The narrator says leaving no survivors was David's mishpat the whole time he lived in Philistine territory. The word is quietly pointed: the one who will one day be the king responsible for justice in Israel has, for now, a custom of killing witnesses.

Aman, to be firm or to trust. Achish trusted David. The verb is often used of trusting God, which makes its use here ironic: Achish places his confidence in a man who is deceiving him, while David, in verse 1, has stopped speaking of trust in the LORD at all.

christ: This chapter offers no prediction of Christ, and it is better not to force one. Its connection to the larger story is the honest portrait of David as a flawed and fearful man even while he is God's chosen king. Israel's hope did not rest on David's moral perfection, and the Bible never pretends it did. That honesty prepares for the later longing for a son of David who would be what David was not: a king who trusts his Father without wavering, never deceives (1 Peter 2:22 says no deceit was found in his mouth), and does not shed innocent blood to save himself, but gives his own life for others.

hard.q: How can the Bible's hero massacre whole communities and lie to cover it?
hard.a: The difficulty is real. David kills men and women alike, not in the heat of battle but to prevent witnesses, and he lies repeatedly. Readers have answered in several ways. Some note that the peoples named, especially the Amalekites, were under the ban declared against them (Exodus 17:14, 1 Samuel 15), so David's warfare against them is in line with an earlier command, though his motive here is secrecy rather than obedience. Others stress that the narrator reports without approving: Scripture often describes what its heroes did without endorsing it, and the silence about prayer in this chapter hints that David is acting outside God's guidance. Still others see in David's deception a wartime ruse of the kind ancient readers admired in weaker parties outwitting stronger ones. Whatever view one takes, the chapter does not present David's conduct as a model. It shows the moral cost of living a double life, and the consequences begin to arrive in chapter 30, when the Amalekites strike Ziklag.

questions: David made a major decision after talking only to himself. What do you tend to do when fear and fatigue push you to decide quickly?
David's deception worked, at least for a while. What does the chapter suggest about the hidden costs of a double life?
Scripture tells the truth about its heroes. How does that honesty affect your trust in the Bible and your view of your own failures?
